title: The Value of Your Family
paragraphs: One evening a son came to his father and said he wished to ask him a question. The father agreed. Going straight to the point, the boy asked how much money his father earned in an hour of work. The father was unsettled by the question and wanted to know why his son was asking such a thing. The boy said he was merely curious and insisted on an answer. At last the father gave in and said he earned a hundred dollars an hour.

Hearing this, the son lowered his head, was silent a moment, then asked his father to lend him fifty dollars. The request angered the father; thinking the boy would spend the money on some senseless toy or something useless, he refused and ordered him to go to his room and sleep. Without protest the son withdrew to his room and closed the door quietly.

The father paced the room, trying to cool his temper. After a while he grew calm and admitted to himself that it had been wrong to flare up without asking why the boy wanted the money. Conscience-stricken, he went to his son's room, knocked lightly, and asked whether he was asleep. The boy said he was still awake.

The father entered and apologized for his harshness. He confessed that he had taken the day's strain out on his son, held out the fifty dollars, and told him to spend it as he wished. The boy thanked him joyfully, drew from under his pillow the money he had hidden, counted it, and looked at his father. Seeing this, the father grew angry again and asked why, if he already had money, he had asked for more.

The son explained that what he had saved before had not been enough for what he wanted, but now he had exactly a hundred dollars. Then he asked whether he might «buy» an hour of his father's time — begging him to come home early from work the next day and have dinner with him.
Those words shook the father to the core; his eyes filled with tears. He embraced his little son and asked his forgiveness.
What children need most is the attention, love, and time their parents give them and share with them.

title: Weeds Must Be Pulled from the Root
paragraphs: When we were schoolchildren we spent our summer holidays with the family in our garden. My late father wanted to harden us to labour. On the days he was at work he left the garden chores to us. He had planted a vegetable patch, and watering it was our duty as well. Because the water from our well was unfit to drink, we would also fetch drinking water from the well in the garden of our neighbour, Uncle Agasalim.

We had learned to dig the soil with a spade. We did the weeding too: with the spade we turned the earth over and crushed and broke the weeds. Yet they were not so easily cleared away. One day Father called us to him and explained: «If you want to destroy a weed, drive the spade deep; the work is not done until you tear out the roots.»
If you do not pull a problem — or a bad habit — out by the root, surface cleanliness is a deception; before long it will raise its head again.

title: A Mother's Love
paragraphs: Erich Fromm
I am 1 — I am so happy; Mother is with me every moment!
I am 2 — Mother is with me now and then (I wonder what is going on?).
I am 3 — Mother is at work; my nanny is with me.
I am 5 — Mother is in a meeting; Grandmother is with me.
I am 7 — Mother is at a seminar; I am at school; my teacher is with me.
I am 13 — I am in adolescence (Mother still has to work); my friends are with me.
I have turned 17 — Mother comes home weary from work. I am in the classroom, at school, in the café; my teacher is with me.
At 20 I am a bright young person — Mother is not at home. My friends are with me.
I have turned 23 and taken a job — Mother is at home now. And I am at work.
I have reached 30 — I wonder... when was the last time Mother and I spent a lovely stretch of time together? There is something strange in this!
I have passed 35; I am married — Mother in her house, I in mine.
I am 40 already... — Mother watches for my coming. Just as I once watched for hers when I was a child...
I have reached 50 — I myself have grown old, yet one wish that never ages remains:
«To join my heart to hers and hold her close, to lay my head upon her knees — those aged, weary knees...»
At 55 I am beside a mother, now for good — the mother of my children!
And my mother... has left this world, and I live with longing for her...
In the familiar flow of life our gravest neglect is that we cannot give our children enough of our time...

Children are the most important players in a magnificent film of life that we could watch without ever growing tired. They change from state to state, colour to colour, form to form. The more we look on them with indifference, the more we will miss the moments that slip past among the swiftly changing frames of life's film.
When we come to see that there is no device with «stop,» «start,» «forward,» and «back» buttons to watch again every moment life has already left behind — God grant it not be too late.
Love your child today, kiss him today, breathe in his scent.
Hold his hands today.
Be with him today.
Watch him today.
Do not miss today's episode for anything!
May you not go into tomorrow with episodes you have not watched,
O beloved mother... O beautiful mother...
«A mother's love is a selfless, sheltering, warm refuge. Because it asks for nothing, nothing can sway it — and it cannot be bought.»
A mother's love is selfless and beyond price. Give time to those you love today, for the only thing you can never give back is time.

title: Mother and Son
paragraphs: The man set the suitcases in his hands down against the wall. Then he straightened, drew a deep breath, and said to his mother: «Mother, this seems a very fine place.» «Of course it is fine, my son,» the elderly woman answered. For a while both were silent, looking carefully about the room.
Then the woman opened her small suitcase and took out a nightgown, slippers, a few towels, and a photograph in a frame. She set the photograph on the table beside her bed.
From the picture a boy in school clothes looked out, standing like a soldier. A child with eyes filled and lips pressed tight...

The man went to the window and drew the curtain. A pale daylight filled the room. Outside there was frost. Resting his hands on the radiator, he watched for a while the cars that passed along the street, muddied and stained. Then, without even turning his head: «Will this wardrobe be enough for you, Mother?» — he asked.
Lost in thought, the elderly woman did not even hear her son. Slightly tilted on the bed, she had fixed her eyes on the shy-eyed child in the worn frame.
It was the photograph they had taken on the first day of school.

Suddenly the woman went back years. Though the day before she had spent hours convincing him how fine a place school was, she had barely managed to get her son into the classroom. She had stayed at the school all day, and at every break had gone to him and said: «I am here, my son; I am waiting for you.» But each time the child clung all the tighter to her hand and wept: «Don't leave me, Mother — I am so afraid.»
The sun was about to set. The man drew his hands from the radiator and leaned against the misted window. «Open your other suitcase too; let's put your things away, Mother,» — he said.

«Don't linger, my son; I will put them away myself. I haven't many things anyway,» — said the elderly woman. With trembling hands she reached out and took her son's hand. It seemed she was about to say something, then she let it go. She swallowed: «The children will be anxious too.»

The door closed with a creak. In the room whose paint was peeling and falling away, the elderly woman was left alone with the shy-eyed, soldier-standing son in the photograph. After sitting a little on the bed she put on her slippers and went to the open-curtained window. Her son was getting into the car.
The elderly woman was afraid. Though the day before she had listened for hours to how fine a place this was, she was afraid.
On the windowpane her son's handprint still remained. Gently she laid her cheek against the mark on the glass. Her eyes filled; her lips pressed tight.
«Don't leave me, my son — I am so afraid,» — she whispered.
The words seemed to strike the misted glass, melt, and flow toward her son, who sat in his car outside and waved to her.

Those who lived on the same floor as the elderly woman heard that night a sobbing cry. And in the old people's home the only thing they were used to was those sobbing voices that wandered the corridors at night.
Life is a circle: the child who one day clings to his mother's hand may tomorrow leave that same mother. True loyalty to a parent is not bodily care alone, but love and attention.

title: Father and Son
paragraphs: After a fierce quarrel with his father the son had left the house in anger. Hurt to the heart, the father too had grown bitter and forbidden even the boy's name to be spoken in the house. As for the mother, every night she sat on her son's bed and fell asleep smelling his pillow.
— I miss my son. Please, let us go and find him and bring him home, — she would say, but the father would not agree.
A long time had passed.
One day, seeing that the mother was forever in tears, the father's pity was moved; from his pocket he drew a scrap of paper with the son's address and held it out to her:
— Go; at this address you can find him, — he said. — But never tell him that I gave you the address.

The father said a few words more, but the mother seemed not to hear him; only the address remained in her mind. She was flying with joy. She made ready at once, set out, and reached the address written on the paper. It was a repair shop. Her son was working in overalls. For several minutes the mother gazed at him with tearful eyes; at last she walked toward him. Long without news of his family, thinking everyone had forgotten him, the son was at first confused when he saw his mother, then held her tight.
He asked after everyone but his father, inquired how they were, and at last:
— How is that man — is he still angry? — he asked his mother.
The mother left the question unanswered and said:
— Come, my son, let us go home.
— No, Mother, I will not go. I cannot live under the same roof with that man again, — he said, and began to walk back toward his workplace.
For a while the mother watched her son from behind, then called to him to give him the sweets she had prepared.
The son took the gift:
— Please, Mother, do not insist; I will not come. I cannot live under the same roof with a man who never once looked for me or took an interest in me, — he said.
With bowed head the mother said:

— Very well, my child; you know best. I see that your decision is firm and you will not return home. But your father asked me to tell you this: keep away from the man you have been friends with this past month — no good will come to you from him. Let him make peace with his old friend, — she said.
Hearing this, the son stood frozen in astonishment.
The mother returned home and reproached the father:
— Husband, if you knew where he was, why did you hide it from me? So that is why you were so at ease?
The father, who always seemed irritable, softened; tears ran from his eyes:
— He is my life, my life, — he said.
— How long have you known? — the mother asked.

— From the day he left. Sometimes at the midday break I would go and watch from a distance to see what he ate and drank. And the reason I sometimes came home late was this: in the evenings I would go and watch our son to learn what he was doing and with whom he kept company, — the father answered.
While the elderly couple clung to each other and wept, there was a knock at the door. Wiping her tears, the mother went to open it.

The son had come home. He kissed his parents' hands and embraced them. He had understood — that the father he had thought had forgotten him, torn him from his heart and cast him away, had in truth never taken his eyes from his child.
Do not hide love — show it. Sometimes a single step taken in time prevents an estrangement that lasts for years.

title: A Father's Footprints
paragraphs: The father to his son:
— Son, mind the steps you take!
The son to his father:
— You mind them, Father! I am following in your footsteps anyway.
The strongest upbringing is example. A child repeats not what you say, but the step you take.

title: Grandfather and Grandson at the Market
paragraphs: Grandfather comes to the supermarket with his grandson. They pass between the shelves, choose groceries, and fill the basket. Meanwhile the grandson now and then shrieks «Buy me that! Buy me this!» and turns the supermarket upside down. Each time Grandfather says, «Be quiet, Arif; we'll finish shopping and go home.» The child reaches the last pitch of his discontent, takes one of the «Kinder Surprise» eggs from the shelf, throws it underfoot and crushes it. Again Grandfather says, «Be quiet, Arif; we'll finish shopping and go home,» then, crestfallen, turns to a nearby clerk: «I am very sorry; I will pay for this as well.»

At last they pay at the till and Grandfather and grandson leave the supermarket. A lady who has witnessed the whole affair follows them out, approaches Grandfather and says: «I am amazed at how you handle Arif. You are a very patient man. Well done!» Grandfather thanks the lady and smiles: «The child's name is Rafiq; Arif is me.»
To keep hold of oneself in a tense moment is a true sign of strength. Keeping one's calm is sometimes not mastering another, but mastering oneself.

title: A Festive Gift
paragraphs: — Elder, — I said, — what shall I buy for the holiday?
He said: — Win the hearts of a few people...
Win a smile from a few children... and
if you can, win the prayer of a few of the poor as well...
The most precious gift is measured not in money but in heart and care. What makes a holiday a holiday is sometimes not what you receive, but what you give.

title: Only My Mother Would Weep
paragraphs: Only my mother weeps; the rest weep for show!
In this world you may see much love, but there is no other love so unconditional and sincere as a mother's.

title: I Am Waiting for the Teeth
paragraphs: On a cold winter evening an elderly couple come in through the door of McDonald's and sit at a table. The man goes to the counter, buys one hamburger, one large box of fries and one large Coca-Cola, and brings them back. He halves the hamburger and sets one half before his wife, and counts out the fries one by one and gives her half. A little later he opens the Coca-Cola bottle, takes a sip himself first, then his wife does.
Those around them were watching and saying «they are sharing a meal for one, the poor things.»
After a while they see that the hamburger and fries before the lady are still untouched. She watches her husband eat with appetite, and now and then takes a sip of the Cola...
At last one of the young workers loses patience, approaches the couple and asks the man:
— Uncle, forgive me — I have been watching you: you are eating, but your wife does not touch the food. If she does not like it, with your leave I will bring her something else...
The elderly man:
— Thank you, young man, but we are content with what we have... We have been married sixty years and we share everything just like this, — he says.
Not satisfied with this answer, the young man this time turns to the lady:
— Dear auntie, why don't you eat your hamburger and fries — what are you waiting for?
The elderly lady points to her husband and answers thus:
— The teeth...! I am waiting for the teeth, my child.
May no one be left in need before the one they love. May God leave no one helpless — not even in their own family.

title: The Mother's Advice Fakir Baykurt Never Forgot
paragraphs: One day Fakir Baykurt (Turkish writer, 1929–1999) asks his mother for tea: «Mother, my heart longs for tea; come, let us drink some tea,» he says. Not wishing to refuse her son, the mother takes him to nearby Topal Hüseyin's teahouse and calls out, «Master, if you please, bring my child a glass of tea.»
When the tea comes, Fakir Baykurt, in the excitement of the moment not knowing how to drink it, takes a great gulp of the hot tea and, burning his mouth, suddenly drops the glass on the ground.
Though the tea glass does not break because it falls on the earth, Fakir Baykurt thinks his mother will slap him. But it is not so. His mother calls Topal Hüseyin and asks him to bring another tea.
This time Baykurt drinks the second tea, blowing on it as he goes. For years he asks his mother why she did not slap him that day, and each time she leaves the question unanswered...

Fakir Baykurt's mother gives the answer to that question years later at the village school where her son is teaching. Fakir Baykurt remembers the day his mother, Elif Hanım, sat in on his lesson thus:
— In class during the lesson I grew angry, I flared up, I thundered! When the lesson ended I asked my mother outside: «Mother dear, how was it — did you like my teaching?»
And Mother said: «Ah, what shall I say, son — it wasn't bad.»
— Mother, the inspectors come, they approve, they give good marks. And you say «it wasn't bad.» How can that be? — I asked.
And Mother spoke these words that could be a lesson to everyone: «For years you asked why I did not slap you. Now I tell you — open your ears and listen!

If I had grown angry the day you spilled the tea, the lion inside you would have sulked. If I had beaten you, that lion would have died! Then you could never have become such a teacher. You behave as I do — stay calm. Do not try to kill the lion inside these children with a stick.»
Do not kill the «lion» inside a child — his self-belief — by beating him. True upbringing is given not by fear, but by patience and love.

title: Spinach
paragraphs: We lived in a remote village. We had no proper road for coming and going. My mother was devoted to spinach. After my father's death, as a child I sometimes suspected she had lost her mind...

«You must eat plenty of it; it gives the body strength,» Mother would say, and for breakfast, lunch and dinner alike she would feed us only spinach, and always with maize bread beside it. I had come to hate spinach; I could not bear the sight of that green.

One day I said to Mother: «When I grow up and have a job and a family, I will never buy spinach for the house. No spinach dish will be cooked at home.» And she promised that she awaited those days impatiently, and that however old she was she would dance at my wedding.

The day came; I left our village for the city to study at secondary school. Somehow I managed on the small stipend I received. When I came home once a month I did not want even a spoonful of the spinach dish Mother set on the table. I longed to return to the dormitory and eat only fine food.

I studied. When I finished university, my master's and my doctorate on a state loan, Mother was already a bent old woman. When I came to the village with the girl I was to marry and we held the wedding, aged Mother both wept and, as she had promised years before, danced at my wedding. At the time I could not understand why Mother shed tears as she danced.
Years passed. Mother died two years ago.

One day in Mother's old chest I found the diary she kept in those days. On one page Mother had written: «All I had left was spinach seed. I kept sowing and tending spinach, and a little maize. There was nothing in hand, nothing in the palm. So that my children would not go hungry I kept cooking and giving them this dish. But I did not rebel. When I said «Spinach is very wholesome; that is why I give you this dish three times a day,» my heart ached. For my little ones this was all I could do. I love them more than my own life.»

At fifty I came to love spinach dishes. My wife keeps asking in surprise why I buy spinach for the house so often, and thinks I simply love spinach. But she does not know that every time I catch the scent of that dish I remember the sacrifices Mother made to raise me, and how she danced at my wedding while she wept...
A mother's sacrifice in want we often understand only years later. Love is sometimes hidden in a plate of simple food.

title: From a Wise Father's Advice to His Son
paragraphs: O my beloved son!
In every child of man there must be a mind fit for forming varied relations with others. That mind is the inexhaustible source of all prosperity and happiness.
One cannot be sated with life; whether it is short or long does not lessen its worth.
Fruit leaves the branch finely only when it is ripe. Likewise, among people they have always preferred those who have seen days and gained experience.
The son of man usually commits the faults of his youth without thinking them through. Yet later, when he remembers them, those offences pierce his heart like a dagger and oppress his soul.
Those who walk the right and good path in youth receive in return honour and esteem in old age.
It is good to be strong and powerful. Yet strength must be placed under the command of the mind.
The Most High God, Creator of the worlds, did not send the child of man into this world to live forever, but willed that at life's end he should taste death.

Know this well too: two things that the Most High God has kept me sound in until this age I have thoroughly tested and made a habit. One is to eat little; the other is to walk about in order to digest what I have eaten.
I wish you to know this as well: in this world there are three kinds of people:
The first — people whose mind and thought are in place, who see and consider the future more or less;

The second — those far from knowing whether their path is straight or crooked, yet who have fallen into this state not by their own wish but under the influence of those around them. When counselled they accept; they listen to words.
And the third — who neither know anything themselves nor heed the counsel given them, and who moreover fancy they know everything. These are the most wretched of all.
O son!
If the Most High God has made you one of those I counted in the first rank, I shall rejoice.
If you are of the second, I advise you to listen to the counsel given you.
Be by no means of the third. They are in no good standing either before God or before men.
The mind is the source of happiness, and strength is the servant of the mind. He who heeds counsel is raised up; he who fancies he knows everything perishes.

title: Puppies for Sale
paragraphs: Seeing a paper stuck to the shop window that said «we have puppies for sale,» a little boy went into the shop:
— How much are the puppies? — he asked.
— Between thirty and fifty dollars. Each has its own price, — said the shopkeeper.
The little boy put his hand in his pocket, took out all the money he had and laid it before the shopkeeper, then carefully counted it all. At last, in a disappointed voice:
— All my money is thirteen dollars and twenty-seven cents, — he said. Then, drawing a deep breath:
— May I at least see the puppies? — he asked.

The shopkeeper smiled and called to his wife in the back room to bring the puppies. Presently the woman came out, and behind her five sweet, plump little pups. But one of the puppies walked with great difficulty. The child fixed his eyes on that puppy:
— What is wrong with this one? Why can't he walk? — he asked.
— Our vet said the bone of the leg is congenitally defective. He will never walk easily, — the shopkeeper answered.
Hearing this, the child said excitedly:
— I want to buy exactly this puppy, — and when he said so the shopkeeper:
— I don't think you'll want to buy him, my child. If you like, I'll give him to you as a gift, — he said.
It was plain from the little boy's eyes that he was much upset. He looked straight into the shopkeeper's eyes:

— I don't want you to give him to me as a gift. That puppy is worth as much as the others. I can give you thirteen dollars and twenty-seven cents now, but every week I will bring five dollars until the thirty dollars are complete, — he said.
The shopkeeper:
— You really wouldn't want that puppy, my boy. He won't be able to run and play with you like the others, — and when he said so the little boy:

— But we must give him a chance; he is worth as much as every puppy, — he protested. Then he bent and slowly drew up the cuff of his trousers, and showed the foot injured by infantile paralysis, and the iron braces. Then he turned to the man and said softly:
— Dear uncle, I can't run and play either. This puppy and I both need friends who will understand us and stand by us.
Every living being needs a friend who will understand him and stand by him. The one who is different is worth as much as the others; he must be given a chance.

title: Fallen Teeth
paragraphs: A shah sees in a dream that all his teeth have fallen out, and calls a dream-interpreter to ask its meaning. The man answers: «Long live the Shah — this means that all your kinsfolk will die, and you will be the last to die.» The shah grows angry, drives the man away, calls another and puts the same question to him, and receives the answer: «Long live the Shah — you will be the longest-lived in your family.» The shah is much pleased with this answer and rewards the man and sends him on his way.
The same truth can be spoken roughly or finely. A word both wounds and heals — know how to say it.

title: I Am Tired, Mother
paragraphs: — I am tired, Mother...
— Of what, my son?
— Of everything: of working, of friends, of going about, of always bearing the burden of pleasing someone — I am tired, so tired.
— Lay your head on my knee and rest, my son; forget everything for a moment... give me your pains...
— Thank you, Mother; good that you are here; with you I forget my age, my living. Bless you, Mother.
— A mother is the giver of life, my son; I am always beside you.
— Mother, we tire you too — forgive us.
— It is not you who tire me, my son. My weariness is being without a mother. I have no «mother's knee» on which to lay my head, my son... Do not grow weary; know the worth of what you hold...
A mother's embrace is the world's most restful refuge. He who has a mother always finds a place to lay his weariness — know the worth of what you hold.

title: The Builder of the Nest
paragraphs: The nest is built by the female bird.
She who builds the nest and keeps the family standing is the woman. Her labour must be seen and valued.

title: Rotten Seed
paragraphs: After his wife died, the father who called his little son — forever suffering from illnesses — a «rotten seed» looked on him with scorn and gave him to an orphanage.
Years pass.
One day this man sees his grown son before a school. He cannot believe his eyes. Watching with regret his son's brightly shining eyes and sound body, the father says excitedly:
— I did not believe you would recover, that a man would come of you. You have become a sturdy champion. How did this miracle happen? How did you get free of the illnesses? — he addresses his son.
The boy fixes his moist eyes on the father who once scorned him, points to the elderly lady approaching with a smile — the one who adopted him — and says:

— After you said «a rotten seed will not sprout» and gave me to the orphanage, this lady took me as a son and, saying «every seed watered with love will sprout,» never withheld her tender hands from me.
A word either raises or destroys. With a single phrase one can exalt a person or bring him down — every seed watered with love will sprout.

title: Raising Children
paragraphs: In a family there was a boy who would not heed his parents' word. Whatever they said, the child did the opposite. At school too his affairs went poorly. He neither studied his lessons with zest nor fully did his homework. Though his mother grew angry and beat him, it did no good. Though his father shut him in his room and punished him, he could not manage the child.

One day, at her wits' end, as the mother was taking the child to school she met a «bear trainer» on the way. Surrounded by curious onlookers, the trainer beat a tambourine, and the bear with a ring through its nose leapt and danced.
The woman stopped and fell to thinking. She said to herself: «I cannot raise this child, and look how this man has trained his bear!»
Then she approached the bear trainer and asked: — I cannot manage my child; how do you teach this wild animal?
The man smiled: — There is a way for everything. I have my own method of training.
The woman said: — Please, help me.
Looking at the boy, the bear trainer said: — It is no hard task. Leave him to me for a week; I will make him obedient.
The woman was glad and began to take the child to the bear trainer and bring him back every day.

Though only a few days had passed, the child's behaviour began slowly to mend. He no longer contradicted his mother. A week later the child was just as the woman wished. She was very glad. She thanked the bear trainer and prayed many blessings upon him.
The neighbours were much astonished. That disobedient, rebellious child was gone, and in his place had come a quiet, peaceful, well-behaved child.

At school the teacher too was pleased with the change in the child and congratulated the mother. Yet the change did not last long. Though no longer as assertive and angry as before, this time the boy began to steal his classmates' things, to do secret deeds and to tell lies in broad daylight. The teacher telephoned the child's mother and said: «I do not know what you will do, but your child has become very strange. He has begun to steal and to lie.» The woman was much grieved. Distressed, she went to look for the bear trainer but could not find him. The man had left those parts.
Seeing the parents' helplessness, a worldly-wise neighbour said: «Do not worry; I know a man of great heart and wisdom. If you wish, go to him and explain the situation.»

The woman agreed. She took her child and brought him to this wise man. When the man had learned the situation he said: — Give me this fine youth for a week; let me see what I can do. — The woman accepted the offer.
She began to take the child to this wise man and bring him back.

After only two meetings the man was much distressed. He said to the child's mother: — What have you done to this child? I see animal traits in him. — The woman was astonished: — I have done nothing; only, once when the child was very unruly I used to take him to a bear trainer and bring him back.

The man grew very angry: — Do you think an animal trainer can raise a child? Animals are trained by fear, and people by conscience. Animals are sometimes brought to order by beating, cursing and punishing; and if that does not help, they shut them in a dark room and leave them helpless. How could you entrust your own child to an animal trainer?

Then he went on: — Remember that upbringing is not going at a child, but entering his heart and influencing him with tenderness. Take your child and go. Draw near him, kiss and embrace him, listen to him, do not withhold your love from him. The more love you show your child, the more he will soften, see that he has parents who love him, and his trust and affection for you will grow.
— The remedy for your child is neither the bear trainer nor I; only you — the parents, — the wise man finished.
A child is raised not by fear but by love. It is not a trainer or an outsider who raises a child — it is the parent who shows love.

title: Hold My Hand
paragraphs: A little girl and her father are crossing a bridge. A little uneasy, the father asks his daughter to hold his hand:
— My sweet girl, hold my hand well so you don't fall into the river.
The little girl answers:
— No, Father — you hold my hand.
A little bewildered, the father asks with interest:
— What difference does it make?
— A very great difference, — the little girl answers. — If I hold your hand and something happens to me, I might let go. But if you hold my hand, I am sure that whatever happens you will not let go.
The power of love is in not letting go. Rather than wait for those who love you to take your hand, you take theirs firmly.

title: The Most Beautiful Gift
paragraphs: For a father — honour,
for a mother — respect,
for a child — tenderness,
for a spouse — love,
for a friend — loyalty,
for society — service,
